title: THE PROVERBS 31 WOMAN IS FAMOUS—BUT THE WARNING ABOUT SEXUAL DESTRUCTION BEFORE HER STORY IS ALMOST NEVER PREACHED.
paragraphs: THE PROVERBS 31 WOMAN IS FAMOUS—BUT THE WARNING ABOUT SEXUAL DESTRUCTION BEFORE HER STORY IS ALMOST NEVER PREACHED.

Before the Bible describes a woman worth more than rubies, a mother warns her son about the kind of desire that can destroy a king. And what she says may expose something our generation desperately needs to confront.
Everybody wants to talk about the Proverbs 31 woman.
Her virtue. Her beauty. Her strength. Her wisdom. Her business. Her marriage. Her children. Her faith.

Churches preach about her. Christian women aspire to become like her. Men are encouraged to look for her. Social media turns her into inspirational captions, marriage advice, and standards for godly womanhood.
But there is something deeply uncomfortable about the chapter that made her famous.
Before Proverbs 31 ever celebrates a virtuous woman, it warns a man not to destroy himself through sexual recklessness.
Read that again.
Before the description of a faithful wife, there is a warning about destructive desire.
Before the praise of noble character, there is a call to self-control.
Before the chapter tells us what kind of woman is worthy of honor, it confronts what kind of man is capable of ruining his own life.
And perhaps that is why so many people begin reading Proverbs 31 at verse 10.
Because verse 10 inspires us.
But verse 3 confronts us.
And sometimes the Scriptures we skip are the very Scriptures our souls need most.
Imagine a mother looking into the eyes of her son.
Not an ordinary son, but a king. A man with influence, authority, resources, and the power to make decisions that could affect an entire nation.
She knows the dangers surrounding him.
She knows power attracts attention.
She knows that admiration can become temptation, temptation can become entitlement, and entitlement can eventually become destruction.
And she knows something every parent eventually discovers.
You can give your child a crown, but you cannot give him character.
You can prepare him for leadership, but you cannot make his heart love righteousness.
So she speaks.
Not as a politician.
Not as a palace adviser.
But as a mother who refuses to remain silent while her son stands near the edge of a dangerous cliff.

Proverbs 31:1 introduces her words as the teaching King Lemuel received from his mother. The passage does not identify Lemuel with certainty, nor does it name his mother. We should not pretend to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But we know what she said.
And her words still speak.
In Proverbs 31:3, the Hebrew reads:
אַל־תִּתֵּן לַנָּשִׁים חֵילֶךָ וּדְרָכֶיךָ לַמְחוֹת מְלָכִין
ʾAl-titten lanashim ḥeilekha, uderakhekha limḥot melakhin.
A close rendering is:
“Do not give your strength to women, or your ways to that which destroys kings.”
The Hebrew word ḥayil (חַיִל), appearing here as ḥeilekha, carries meanings associated with strength, capability, wealth, or resources.
And the warning is not merely about physical energy.
It concerns what a man gives away.
His strength.
His attention.
His resources.
His integrity.
His capacity to lead wisely.
His ability to remain faithful to the responsibilities entrusted to him.
The language about women must also be understood carefully. This is not a declaration that women are dangerous or that female sexuality is inherently corrupt.
That interpretation would contradict the chapter itself, which goes on to honor a woman of wisdom, dignity, strength, and godly character.
The warning concerns a king surrendering himself to destructive sexual relationships and conduct that undermine his responsibilities.
The problem is not womanhood.
The problem is desire without wisdom, power without restraint, and pleasure pursued at the expense of faithfulness.
And that warning is not limited to men.
Because the human heart has never needed a crown to become intoxicated with what God has forbidden.
Some people are destroying their marriages for a moment of attention.
Some are sacrificing their integrity for a relationship they know they should leave.
Some are carrying secret conversations that would devastate their spouses if the messages were exposed.
Some have learned to quote Scripture publicly while privately negotiating with temptations they refuse to surrender.
Some are not physically unfaithful, but they are cultivating emotional intimacy with someone who is not their husband or wife.
And some have been wounded so deeply by betrayal that merely reading these words brings back memories they have spent years trying to bury.
Perhaps you know that pain.
Perhaps you are the person who was betrayed.
Perhaps you are the one who betrayed someone.
Perhaps nobody knows what you are fighting.
But God does.
And He is not exposing sin in His Word because He delights in humiliation.
He calls sinners into the light because darkness is a terrible place to build a life.
The tragedy of sexual sin is not simply that it breaks a rule.
It can break trust.
It can destroy families.
It can corrupt judgment.
It can turn people into objects to be consumed rather than neighbors to be loved.
It can teach a person to defend deception until lying feels normal.
And it can slowly persuade someone that temporary satisfaction is worth more than lasting faithfulness.
That is the danger King Lemuel's mother wanted him to recognize.
A person may possess tremendous authority over others and still lack authority over his own impulses.
A king may govern a nation while failing to govern himself.
And a Christian may know the language of holiness while resisting the surrender holiness requires.
Think about David.
A man who loved God.
A man who wrote psalms.
A man who experienced divine deliverance and received extraordinary responsibility.
Yet in 2 Samuel 11, David saw Bathsheba, sent for her, and took her while she was married to Uriah.
We must not soften the abuse of royal power in that account or place the blame upon Bathsheba.
David was the king.
David initiated the wrongdoing.
David orchestrated the attempt to conceal it.
And David arranged circumstances that led to Uriah's death.
The consequences were devastating.
David's story is not a warning about the seductive power of women.
It is a warning about what happens when a powerful man treats his desires as more important than God's commands and other people's dignity.
And when the prophet Nathan confronted him, David eventually confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
Those words matter.
Because repentance begins when we stop explaining away what God calls sin.
Not when we blame loneliness.
Not when we blame our spouse.
Not when we blame temptation.
Not when we say everybody does it.
But when we come before God without pretending.
“I have sinned.”
Three words in English that can mark the beginning of a changed life.
And yet the story does not end with David.
Consider Solomon.
A king associated with extraordinary wisdom, yet whose later life became marked by serious spiritual compromise.
According to 1 Kings 11:1–4, Solomon loved many foreign women, and his wives turned his heart toward other gods.
The passage condemns his disobedience and idolatry, not the inherent worth of women from other nations.
The warning is sobering.
You can possess wisdom and still refuse to obey it.
You can recognize danger and still walk toward it.
You can know what God says and still persuade yourself that your situation is somehow an exception.
And perhaps that is one of the most frightening forms of spiritual deception.
Not ignorance.
But knowing the truth while quietly arranging your life around a lie.
Yet Proverbs 31 does not stop at sexual warning.
The mother continues.
In verses 4–5, she warns Lemuel about intoxicating drink and the danger of impaired judgment.
In verses 8–9, she commands him to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves, to judge righteously, and to defend the rights of the poor and needy.
Do you see the connection?
The king must not become enslaved to his appetites because other people depend upon his judgment.
His moral choices are not isolated.
His private conduct can affect public justice.
His self-control is connected to his responsibility toward the vulnerable.
And then comes verse 10.
The passage everyone recognizes.
“Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.” — Proverbs 31:10, KJV
But even here, something beautiful is hidden beneath the familiarity of the English words.
The Hebrew expression is:
אֵשֶׁת־חַיִל
ʾEshet ḥayil.
Often rendered “virtuous woman,” it can also communicate the idea of a woman of strength, excellence, capability, or noble character.
Notice that word again.
Ḥayil.
The same Hebrew noun family associated with the king's strength in verse 3 is used to describe the excellent woman in verse 10.
The connection is striking, even though we should be careful not to claim that the entire chapter rests upon this single repeated word.
The king is warned against giving away his strength in destructive relationships.
Then the poem celebrates a woman characterized by strength and excellence.
One passage warns against moral ruin.
The other honors faithful character.
And together they challenge the shallow way we sometimes talk about relationships.
Because Proverbs 31 is not teaching men to demand perfection from women while excusing their own lack of discipline.
Nor is it teaching women that their worth depends upon becoming exhausted, endlessly productive, or flawless.
The woman described in Proverbs 31:10–31 is not a social media performance.
She is a poetic portrait of wisdom expressed through faithful living.
The passage is an alphabetic acrostic in Hebrew, with its twenty-two verses beginning successively with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet.
It presents a comprehensive literary celebration of excellent character, not a checklist by which every woman must be measured every morning.
She works diligently.
She acts wisely.
She cares for her household.
She engages in productive enterprise.
She extends her hands to the needy.
She speaks with wisdom and kindness.
And above all, she fears the LORD.
Proverbs 31:30 declares:
“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.” — KJV
That is the foundation.
Not appearance.
Not popularity.
Not wealth.
Not an impressive online image.
The fear of the LORD.
And that is not a principle reserved for women.
It is the foundation of biblical wisdom for everyone.
A man who fears the LORD cannot justify exploiting women.
A woman who fears the LORD is not called to excuse betrayal or abuse in the name of submission.
A husband who fears the LORD must learn to love sacrificially.
A wife who fears the LORD is worthy of dignity and honor.
And a single believer who fears the LORD is not spiritually incomplete because marriage has not happened.
The Gospel does not divide humanity into the married people who matter and the unmarried people who are waiting to matter.
Our deepest identity is not found in our relationship status.
It is found in our relationship with Jesus Christ.
And this is where the message becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have spent years searching for a Proverbs 31 spouse while refusing to become a person of Proverbs-shaped character.
We want someone faithful while entertaining secret unfaithfulness.
We want someone honest while concealing our own compromises.
We want someone prayerful while neglecting prayer.
We want someone who fears God while keeping certain parts of our lives outside His authority.
We ask God to send someone trustworthy.
But have we become trustworthy?
We ask God to protect our future marriage.
But are we protecting our present integrity?
We ask God for a relationship that honors Christ.
But do our private decisions honor Him now?
These are uncomfortable questions.
They should be.
Because biblical wisdom does not exist merely to make us admire righteousness from a distance.
It calls us to live differently.
And yet there is another danger here.
The danger of turning this chapter into a weapon.
A weapon against women who are already exhausted.
A weapon against husbands who are struggling to grow.
A weapon against people carrying shame from sexual sins they have already confessed and abandoned.
A weapon against those whose marriages collapsed despite their sincere efforts to remain faithful.
A weapon against survivors of exploitation who were never responsible for the wrongdoing committed against them.
That is not what this passage was given to accomplish.
Scripture confronts sin.
But Scripture must never be twisted to excuse cruelty.
Jesus Christ never treated sexual sin as harmless.
Yet He also refused to reduce human beings to their worst moments.
Remember the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus knew the complicated truth about her relationships.
He did not need her to perform innocence.
He did not pretend her circumstances were irrelevant.
But neither did He treat her as a disposable person.
He spoke to her about living water.
He revealed Himself to her.
And the woman who had come to draw water left with news she could not keep to herself.
She went back to her community and told people about Jesus.
The story is not merely about a woman with a difficult relational history.
It is about the Messiah revealing Himself and offering life.
That is the center of the Gospel.
Not that sinners are impressive.
Not that our past is harmless.
Not that repentance is optional.
But that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And when we turn to Him, we discover that grace is neither permission to remain in bondage nor a reward for pretending we were never broken.
Grace meets us in truth.
And grace calls us into transformation.
Listen to the words of the apostle Paul.
In 1 Corinthians 6:18, he commands believers to flee sexual immorality.
The Greek phrase is:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The verb pheugete is an imperative, a command to flee.
Not entertain it.
Not test how close you can get.
Not keep the conversation going because you think you are spiritually strong enough.
Flee.
Sometimes fleeing means ending the private conversation.
Sometimes it means deleting the secret account.
Sometimes it means confessing deception and seeking accountability.
Sometimes it means leaving a relationship that continually pulls you away from obedience to Christ.
Sometimes it means seeking pastoral guidance or professional help for entrenched patterns of sexual behavior.
And sometimes it means finally admitting that what you have been calling a harmless friendship has become an emotional betrayal.
But do not misunderstand.
Fleeing sin is not the same as fleeing a person who has been victimized.
If someone has been coerced, assaulted, manipulated, or abused, the responsibility belongs to the perpetrator. Seeking safety and trustworthy support is not a failure of faith.
God's call to holiness must never be used to silence those who have suffered injustice.
And for the person who knows they have sinned, there is still hope.
Real hope.
Not the cheap hope of pretending nothing happened.
Not the false hope of avoiding consequences.
But the costly hope purchased by Jesus Christ.
Because the same chapter of 1 Corinthians that warns about sexual immorality also reminds believers of the transforming work of God.
After naming various patterns of sinful living, Paul writes:
Such were some of you.
Not because their past never existed.
Not because sin suddenly became righteous.
But because the grace of God had reached them.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not by their own moral résumé.
But in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God.
Perhaps you need to hear that tonight.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because you have fallen.
You are not beyond His mercy because you have failed more than once.
You are not beyond forgiveness because your sin became public.
And you do not have to invent a spotless past before approaching the Savior who already knows the truth.
But neither should you confuse forgiveness with an excuse to keep returning deliberately to the same destructive choices.
Jesus calls us to repentance.
To turn away from sin and toward Him.
To bring our secrets into His light.
To surrender what has been controlling us.
And to learn obedience through the power of His Spirit.
Some consequences may remain.
Some relationships may require years of rebuilding.
Some trust may never be restored in the way we hoped.
Grace does not guarantee that every person we wounded will reconcile with us.
But grace does mean that our failure does not have to be the final authority over who we become.
And that brings us back to the mother in Proverbs 31.
I wonder how many tears were behind her instruction.
The text does not tell us.
We do not know whether she spoke from personal grief, observed tragedy, prophetic wisdom, or ordinary maternal concern.
We should not invent a biography for her.
But we can recognize the love expressed in the warning.
Because genuine love does not always sound like applause.
Sometimes love says, “Do not go there.”
Sometimes love says, “That relationship is destroying you.”
Sometimes love says, “Your family needs your faithfulness more than your reputation needs protecting.”
Sometimes love says, “Stop hiding.”
Sometimes love says, “Come back to God.”
And perhaps someone reading this has been resisting such a warning for months.
You know the conversation you need to end.
You know the confession you have been postponing.
You know the boundary you keep crossing.
You know the spiritual compromise you have dressed up with religious language.
And the Holy Spirit may be using the plain truth of Scripture to confront you right now.
Do not harden your heart.
Not because God is waiting for an opportunity to crush you.
But because the Savior who died for sinners is worthy of your surrender.
You do not need another inspirational quote that leaves your life unchanged.
You need Jesus.
Not merely as a religious symbol.
Not merely as someone you mention when life becomes difficult.
But as Lord.
As Savior.
As the One who has authority over your relationships, your body, your decisions, your money, your words, your ambitions, and the secret places of your heart.
Because Christianity is not about looking respectable while quietly making peace with sin.
It is about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ and learning to walk in newness of life.
And here is something the Proverbs 31 conversation desperately needs.
The virtuous woman is not the savior of an undisciplined man.
A godly wife cannot repent on behalf of her husband.
A faithful husband cannot manufacture holiness inside his wife.
Marriage cannot do what only Christ can do.
You can marry someone beautiful and remain spiritually empty.
You can marry someone hardworking and remain unfaithful.
You can marry someone deeply devoted to God and still resist His Word yourself.
A spouse is not a substitute for surrender.
And if you are unmarried, you do not have to wait for a wedding to begin living faithfully.
Your calling to holiness is already real.
Your dignity is already real.
Your responsibility before God is already real.
And your worth in Christ is not postponed until someone chooses you.
The deepest question of Proverbs 31 is not simply, “Where can I find a virtuous woman?”
It is also, “Am I becoming a person shaped by the wisdom and fear of the LORD?”

Because when the chapter is read from beginning to end, it challenges the desires of the powerful, defends the vulnerable, honors excellent character, and directs our attention toward reverence for God.
And when we read it in the light of the whole Bible, it ultimately exposes our need for someone greater than Lemuel.
Greater than Solomon.
Greater than David.
Someone who never surrendered His righteousness to temptation.
Someone who used His authority not to exploit the vulnerable but to serve and save.
Someone who did not take advantage of the weak but gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus Christ.
The true King.
The faithful Son.
The sinless Savior.
The One who was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
The One who gave His life as a ransom for many, as Mark 10:45 declares.
The One who rose again so that those who trust in Him might receive forgiveness and new life.
This is why the Gospel is greater than self-improvement.
Because our greatest problem is not that we have failed to become the perfect Proverbs 31 man or woman.
Our greatest problem is sin.
And our greatest hope is Christ.
We do not earn salvation by achieving flawless moral discipline.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
Yet Ephesians 2:10 immediately reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves us.
And the grace that saves us also begins changing how we live.
That is why repentance matters.
That is why holiness matters.
That is why faithfulness matters.
Not because we are trying to purchase God's love.
But because, in Christ, we have received a love that changes everything.
Maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Maybe you are thinking about the marriage you damaged.
The trust you broke.
The person you used.
The temptation you entertained.
The warning you ignored.
Or perhaps you are remembering how someone else's sin shattered your sense of safety.
If that is you, please hear this carefully.
The cross of Jesus Christ is not a declaration that your suffering was insignificant.
It is the place where God's justice and mercy are revealed with breathtaking seriousness.
Sin is so serious that Christ bore its judgment.
Grace is so extraordinary that Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
And resurrection means death and darkness do not have the final word.
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
But in Christ, yesterday does not have to dictate every tomorrow.
So pray.
Not with polished religious language.
Not with a performance designed to impress other believers.
Just speak to Him.

“Lord Jesus, You know the truth about me. You know what I have hidden, what I have justified, what I have suffered, and what I have done. Forgive my sins. Heal what is broken. Give me courage to repent, wisdom to make things right where I can, and strength to walk in obedience. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. I cannot save myself. I need Your mercy, Your truth, and Your transforming grace. Amen.”
And if this message exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to reveal private details publicly to prove your repentance.
But you can take one honest step.
Not as a performance.
Not to earn approval.
But as a reminder that nobody should have to pretend they are spiritually invincible.
We need one another.
We need prayer.
We need biblical truth.
We need repentance.
We need encouragement.
And above everything else, we need Jesus Christ.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious content for a few seconds before they return to the same spiritual emptiness.
But to keep placing Scripture, conviction, encouragement, and the hope of the Gospel before people who desperately need truth.
There are believers who are hungry for God's Word but do not know where to begin.
There are families struggling to raise their children in the faith.
There are Christians trying to rebuild their lives after failure.
There are seekers asking whether Jesus could really forgive someone like them.
And there are people who may never walk into a church building today but might encounter a Scripture-centered message on their Facebook feed.
That is why your sharing matters.
Not merely because you agree with it.
But because someone connected to you may be standing at the very crossroads this passage describes.
Someone may be about to sacrifice a marriage for a secret relationship.
Someone may be wondering whether forgiveness is still possible.
Someone may be blaming themselves for betrayal they never deserved.
Someone may be searching for a reason to return to Christ.
You do not know who might read it.
And you do not know what God may do through His Word.
Because temptation rarely announces itself as destruction.
Sometimes it arrives as flattery.
Sometimes as loneliness.
Sometimes as a seemingly innocent conversation.
Sometimes as the comforting lie that nobody will ever know.
And when those moments come, you may need to remember the warning that stood before the famous Proverbs 31 woman.
And for those who believe in this mission and have the means to help it continue, I want to extend a personal invitation.
But let us keep something biblically clear.
The Bible teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
God's favor cannot be bought.
And financial hardship does not make anyone less faithful.
You can honor Christ by praying, serving, sharing His Word, caring for people in need, and supporting sound ministry in ways appropriate to your circumstances.
These products can be reminders of faith, conversation starters, and resources for encouragement, but the real purpose of this ministry will always be greater than merchandise.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
It is about helping believers grow.
It is about bringing biblical truth into places where confusion, compromise, shame, and spiritual exhaustion have taken root.
And it is about remembering that every person who encounters the Gospel is more important than any number on a screen.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build a following around a page.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
And that brings us to the question we began with.
Why does the famous chapter about the virtuous woman begin with a warning about destructive desire?
Because wisdom is not merely about recognizing the beauty of godly character in someone else.
It is about allowing God's truth to confront the desires within ourselves.
Because a beautiful relationship without faithfulness is fragile.
Because authority without self-control is dangerous.
Because religious knowledge without obedience can become a mask.
Because outward admiration of virtue is not the same as inward surrender to God.
And because the God who calls us to holiness is also the God who provides forgiveness and transforming grace through His Son.
So the next time someone quotes Proverbs 31:10, remember Proverbs 31:3.
Remember the mother who warned her son.
Remember the king who needed wisdom.
Remember the vulnerable people whose well-being depended upon righteous leadership.
Remember the woman whose true excellence was rooted in the fear of the LORD.
And above all, remember Jesus Christ.
The King who never failed.
The Savior who died for those who have.
The Lord who calls us to repent.
The Redeemer who makes new life possible.
The Proverbs 31 woman deserves to be honored.
But the warning before her description deserves to be heard.
And the Christ to whom all Scripture ultimately directs us deserves more than our admiration.
He deserves our faith.
Our repentance.
Our obedience.
Our worship.
Our lives.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that you once fell into sin—it is to hear the voice of grace calling you home and choose to remain where sin left you.
